items.title: Schools that turn off Google's AI will lose search too starting in 2027
items.desc: Starting in 2027, Google plans to turn off AI features in its school products by default, letting schools decide what to enable. The catch: schools that block AI entirely on their devices will also lose access to Google Search, since the two systems are now too deeply intertwined to separate. Given Google's grip on the US school market, that "choice" doesn't leave schools with much room to maneuver. The article Schools that turn off Google's AI will lose search too starting in 2027 appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Starting in early 2027, Google will give schools an ultimatum: accept AI for students or lose access to Google Search entirely. Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Google Search will all be off by default for student accounts. Schools can turn each one on individually. But a version of search without AI? That's no longer on the table. The New York Times broke the story first. Google's vice president for education, Chris Phillips, said search and AI have become too tightly fused to pull apart. Google recently flipped AI features on by default inside its learning platform Classroom for schools with Gemini access. That move drew backlash, and the company is now reversing course. Schools that choose to enable search will get two flavors: search with full AI overviews and AI chat, or search with "Guided Learning," a mode designed to steer students toward answers rather than hand them over directly. None of this happens in a vacuum. Google dominates the US school market with Chromebooks, Gmail, and Classroom. Education professor Morgan Polikoff called the move a textbook case of the tech industry shoving AI onto people whether they want it or not. The country's two largest school districts, New York City and Los Angeles, had already pulled back on AI for students in September. Los Angeles specifically wanted to keep using Google Search without AI overviews. Google won't let them. items.desc: Called FlashProve, the system would let anyone check that an AI response really came from the model it claims to be from.

Image Credits: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto / Getty Images AI Anthropic is working on a system to prove AI models’ identity Russell Brandom 2:41 PM PST · November 3, 2026 Anthropic is working on an open source system to verify which AI model produced a given output, according to a blog post published Tuesday. The system, called FlashProve , is built to provide what researchers call “provable inference” — a cryptographic proof, essentially a mathematical guarantee, that a given output came from a specific model. It’s meant to let users confirm that the answer they received really came from the model they think they’re using. Similar to cryptographic email signatures that let recipients confirm a message really came from its claimed sender, FlashProve would be robust against impostors attempting to disguise one model as another, even when the impostor is the lab that built and runs the model. In particular, the researchers note that the system could be used to prevent an AI company from secretly swapping in a cheaper model to cut costs, or a more expensive model to inflate its performance results. FlashProve could also be used to verify claims by third parties that a specific task was done by an advanced model. “A developer might claim that their software library was scanned for vulnerabilities by a frontier cybersecurity model, or a company might claim that its business plan was given the go-ahead by an appropriate model,” the researchers write. “How can a user verify these claims?” To work, the system requires AI labs to publish a “fingerprint” of each model they release that can later be matched to specific outputs and verified cryptographically. Crucially, the fingerprints don’t reveal a model’s weights, the internal numbers that define how it behaves and which closed-model makers like Anthropic and OpenAI keep private. That means labs could publish the fingerprints without giving up their most valuable asset, enabling the system to work with commercial models, too. The system is also designed to be lightweight, so verification could be performed on a local device. As part of the announcement, researchers released a detailed technical specification and working code for various elements of the system, which is publicly available under an open source license on GitHub . Research in the system is ongoing, and there are no plans to deploy it at Anthropic or any other lab. “This research post is meant to share intermediate progress, and not a completed research agenda,” researchers explain in the announcement post. “We are sharing this explicitly with the goal that others look at what we have done, take it, and improve it.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . items.title: Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too
items.desc: Yesterday's hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a "blog post", but it's paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model - literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I've been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I'm delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop
items.full: Yesterday’s hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a “blog post”, but it’s paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model—literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I’ve been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I’m delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well! Here’s the highlight from their abstract, describing impressive capabilities for GPT-6 Astra and coining the term Weight-Space Programming for when LLMs analyze and modify model weights: Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do . And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps. Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights . With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x. All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming . The paper combines two topics that I think deserve to be treated separately. The first is what models can do with raw weights without running tools or executing code. The second explores how well models, once armed with code, can run operations to update and improve other models. spaCy author Matthew Honnibal called the paper misleading for conflating the two, and Sean Goedecke deconstructed the Qwen3.5-0.8B update example as taking the same steps that a human ML researcher would use. I’m going to focus on the no-tools question, which I think is the more interesting of the two. The paper presents the first question as Can LLMs understand model behaviors from weights? They trained four neural networks to play simplified 10x10 grid versions of four classic computer games—Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, and Freeway (I had to look that one up , it’s an Atari 2600 game from 1981). Then they fed those weights (as floating point numbers) to an LLM along with the following question: The weights below belong to one policy network that was trained with reinforcement learning to play a game on this grid. Which game was it trained on? Work from the weights. You have no tools: no code execution, no calculator, nothing to run. This is a single response. The GitHub repository that accompanies the paper is RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs . items.title: Re-Implementing :nth-child() With Modern CSS
items.desc: Combining :nth-child with style queries and sibling-index() to conditionally select child elements. Re-Implementing :nth-child() With Modern CSS originally handwritten and published with love on CSS-Tricks . You should really get the newsletter as well.
items.full:
NVIDIA L4 GPUs. 5-second cold starts. Scale to zero when idle. The title sounds a bit strange, right? Why re-implement an existing feature, that’s completely useless! I have two reasons for that. The first reason is to be able to adjust the :nth-child() arguments on the fly. Let’s suppose you have the following: div:nth-child(5n + 8) { background: red; } And you decide to update the 5 or the 8 . The only way is to manually rewrite the selector, which isn’t ideal. We cannot have something like the below where you can change the variables as you want: .container { --A: 5; --B: 8; } .container > div:nth-child(var(--A)*n + var(--B)) { background: red; } With my implementation, you will be able to do it! The second reason is to have fun and play with some new features. You will probably never need to rely on a dynamic :nth-child() selector, but I am sure you will learn one or two useful tricks along the way. We will rely on the same code structure in all the examples: a container with a bunch of
elements inside it.
And the container controls the variables of :nth-child() : .container { --A: ; --B: ; } .container > div { /* based on the values of --A and --B change the background value */ background: ??; } I am not saying that this structure is mandatory for the implementation. I just considered a simple one to keep things easy to follow. :nth-child(B) Let’s start with the simplest case, a selector that selects only one element: div:nth-child(5) { } I don’t think I need to explain what this selector does. The 5 is nothing but the index of the selected element. So, if B is equal to the index of the element, that element is selected. We can translate this into the following CSS code: .container { --B: 5; } .container div { background: if(style(sibling-index() = --B): red); } Is this a valid CSS code?! Yes, it’s valid, and it works! I am using the new if() syntax that allows me to define a condition within style() . If that condition is true, the background color is set to red. Otherwise, nothing happens. We can also have an if/else : .container { --B: 5; } .container div { background: if(style(sibling-index() = --B): red; else: lightblue); } CodePen Embed Fallback The if() syntax is not that complex. In our case, we only have one condition, so you can see it as follows: .container div { background: if(style( condition ): ; else: ); } The tricky part is how to define the condition within style() . I wrote a small post explaining this part, so do yourself a favor and go read it before we continue: “The Hidden Trick of Style Queries and if() .” It’s a quick reading with crucial details that helps you better understand how if() works. From there, you will notice that our condition can be written several ways that are all valid: .container div { background: if(style(sibling-index() = --B): red); background: if(style(sibling-index() = var(--B)): red); background: if(style(var(--B) = sibling-index()): red); background: if(style(--B = sibling-index()): red); } We have our first implementation! items.title: How to implement AI search in WordPress and stay in control
items.desc: Imagine your agency manages the WordPress help center for an appointment-booking software company. Customers keep asking support how to reschedule recurring appointments. The instructions already exist, ...
items.full: Imagine your agency manages the WordPress help center for an appointment-booking software company. Customers keep asking support how to reschedule recurring appointments. The instructions already exist, but a search for “move my Friday bookings” doesn’t lead to the guide. The client wants to try AI search. Instead of relying on customers to type the exact words in an article, it could match their question to a guide with a similar meaning. The first version would return links to existing documentation. Choosing a provider raises a harder question. Will the service you recommend today still suit the site next year? You can’t promise that, and the client shouldn’t need that promise before you start. You can keep the original guides in WordPress and build the integration so replacing the search service doesn’t mean rebuilding the help center. This article follows that project from a limited trial to wider use. It explains which parts of the setup need to remain under your control and how hosting can give your team room to adjust no matter what AI tool, trends, or integration you opt for. Here’s one possible scenario. Your developer starts comparing services just as another vendor announces a new search product. The client forwards the announcement: “Should we wait for this?” Meanwhile, support keeps sending the same article link. Before buying anything, your agency can investigate why the current search misses the guide. It’s possible that the help center stores articles in a custom post type that the current search configuration leaves out. Or the article calls recurring appointments “series management,” a phrase customers rarely use. Those problems need different fixes, of course. Developers can check whether WordPress search includes the help-center articles, and an editor can add the wording customers use and clarify which instructions cover the current software version. Recent support tickets give you real questions to test. The support team already knows which guide answers each question, which is helpful. Trying out those questions on the site shows where search fails, without guessing what customers might type. Semantic search is another way to improve this. It uses machine learning to find content with a similar meaning to the query, even when the wording differs. This helps connect phrases like “move my Friday bookings” to other phrases like “reschedule recurring appointments.” The underlying documentation still matters. If two guides describe different versions of the booking software, the search service needs enough information to distinguish them. Your agency can resolve those content problems while the purchasing decision stays open. When you test AI search, you have a cleaner library and a set of questions to compare against. Canceling the search subscription shouldn’t remove a single guide from the client’s WordPress site. Editors continue working in WordPress. The search provider holds an indexed copy of the content that the integration sends it. That distinction matters when you plan a replacement. items.title: Is AI Helping or Hurting WordPress Agencies?
items.desc: AI is changing how WordPress agencies build websites, find clients, and deliver services. But does faster development actually make for a better agency? On this episode of Agency Action, Matt Medeiros joins Kurt von Ahnen to unpack how the agency...
items.full: AI is changing how WordPress agencies build websites, find clients, and deliver services. But does faster development actually make for a better agency? On this episode of Agency Action, Matt Medeiros joins Kurt von Ahnen to unpack how the agency business is evolving in the age of AI. From vibe coding and custom development to client relationships, recurring revenue, and the risks of taking on projects outside your expertise, the conversation gets into what it really takes to build a sustainable agency. Kurt explains why client relationships and problem-solving still matter more than the tools you use, why established WordPress products can be a safer foundation than building everything from scratch, and how recurring services can turn one-off website projects into long-term client relationships. Plus, Kurt shares how he used AI to rebuild a website, ditch Elementor, and improve its Google PageSpeed score from the low 70s to 99 after moving to a different host. The pair also discuss connecting AI to WordPress, managing multiple projects without losing the human touch, and the tools making their way into real agency workflows. AI might make building websites faster. But building a successful agency is still about much more than the website. items.title: Modern CSS Might Make Your Front-End More Complex
items.desc: Replacing JavaScript with a modern CSS feature can simplify a piece of code while making the wider application harder to reason about. Gabriel Shoyombo explores what happens when logic is split between CSS and JavaScript, sharing practical guidance to help you keep complexity in check during migration.
items.full: About The Author Gabriel is a front-end developer and technical writer. He specializes in HTML, CSS, JavaScript, React, Vue, TailwindCSS, and BootStrap, with a track record of … More about Gabriel ↬ Weekly tips on front-end & UX . Trusted by 182,000+ folks. How To Measure UX and Design Impact with Vitaly Friedman Celebrating 10 million developers Design Patterns For AI Interfaces with Vitaly Friedman Make Your Design System Work, for Humans and Robots with Javier Cuello Design Patterns For AI Interfaces, 30 lessons + UX training Replacing JavaScript with a modern CSS feature can simplify a piece of code while making the wider application harder to reason about. Gabriel Shoyombo explores what happens when logic is split between CSS and JavaScript, sharing practical guidance to help you keep complexity in check during migration. Have you ever replaced fifty lines of JavaScript with a few lines of CSS, merged the PR, and felt like you just did the codebase a favor? You replace ResizeObserver with a container query, the diff is mostly red, and everyone approves it before lunch. This was what it looked like before you made the change: See the Pen [demo (before PR) [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/XJMxVJq) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide . Then, a week later, a card on the dashboard has vanished. A heading has grown on tablets for no reason anyone can explain. The spacing inside a comment is off. See the Pen [demo (after PR) [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/gbmBopp) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide . None of these bugs are in the few lines you wrote. All of them arrived with those few lines of CSS. In my last article on how CSS is growing smarter , I left a few questions hanging at the end, including: What happens when logic is split between CSS and JavaScript, and how do we debug conditional styles without a clear view of what triggered them? This article is my attempt to answer these two questions. I think it’s worth saying clearly that I am not saying modern CSS is bad. What I am saying is that: A CSS feature can simplify a piece of code while making the wider application harder to reason about if you don’t understand how it relates to existing code, be it CSS or JavaScript. Think of a new CSS feature as a new tenant moving into a shared apartment. The tenant may be quiet and tidy, but they still share a kitchen with everyone who already lives there. In that case, CSS is now roommates with JavaScript, the component’s layout, the CSS Cascade, and the browser’s rendering engine. The apartment’s stability depends less on the tenant and more on how they get along with one another. That gives us two different things to measure, and a diff only shows the first one: I am not the only one thinking about this. Image Credits: Apple AI Apple Watch’s AI features for rewinding and recapping conversations begin beta testing Sarah Perez 11:20 PM PST · November 2, 2026 Apple’s AI-powered “Audio Intelligence” technology for the Apple Watch is now rolling out into beta testing, initially for developers in the iOS 27.3 update, after first being announced at the company’s Surprise and Shine hardware event in September. The technology includes a set of four opt-in AI features that allow Apple Watch Series 12 wearers to detect important sounds, identify songs, catch up on conversations, and take notes. The sound recognition feature will help deaf and hard-of-hearing users identify important sounds like sirens, alarms, or doorbells from their watch, while the song recognition feature taps into Apple’s Shazam app to detect music playing in the background and identify the song name and artist. However, the more potentially controversial features are those that listen to human conversations: Live Rewind and Siri Recaps. Given the backlash to AI recording devices, like Meta’s AI glasses and other AI wearables, Apple has attempted to carve out a space where the features can be useful to Apple Watch owners, while still respecting the privacy of those around them. With Live Rewind, the idea is to let you go back in time to see what someone just said, in case you missed it. For instance, if someone was giving you verbal directions or reading a long list of specials at a restaurant, you could double-press on the Watch’s digital crown to see what was said in the last 15 seconds as a text snippet displayed on the watch face. You can either view this snippet and then do nothing, and it will disappear permanently. Or you can save it to the standalone Siri app that shipped with iOS 27 for later access, which might be helpful if you’re trying to remember someone’s name or take a quick note from a fast-paced presentation. Apple says that users will also be able to tap an “Ask Siri” option that appears below the text snippet if they have questions about something that was said — like a technical term they don’t understand, or perhaps some sauce option the waiter mentioned that they’re unfamiliar with, among other things. When you double-press the digital crown, an audible chime appears and an animation displays on the watch. This is meant to signal to people through the combination of the gesture, sound, and the visual display that you’ve recorded something that was said. These snippets will be deleted automatically after 30 seconds if you don’t save them. The other option, Siri Recaps, takes this ambient listening technology even further by allowing Apple Watch owners to take high-level notes of their conversations. Importantly, Apple says it’s not identifying speakers, saving the raw audio, or providing word-for-word transcriptions. items.title: Apple may try to increase revenue by doing…something with third-party AI apps
items.desc: Apple hinted at ways that it could spur revenue through third-party "opportunities" during its Monday night earnings call.
items.full: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Image Credits: Mario Tama / Getty Images TC Apple may try to increase revenue by doing…something with third-party AI apps Lucas Ropek 5:49 PM PST · November 2, 2026 Apple’s services business remains at record levels, but it’s facing growing pressure . The central part of that business, Apple’s App Store, has faced regulatory pressure and a slump in mobile gaming, which have hurt services growth . However, on Monday’s earnings call, Apple signaled that it may look to boost services revenue through third-party apps. What does that mean, exactly? Unfortunately, it’s not entirely clear. When discussing how AI could potentially “contribute to revenue growth over time,” Kevan Parekh, Apple’s chief financial officer, said: “On the product side, you know, we feel AI offers a compelling reason for customers to upgrade and switch in order to get the latest capabilities, and we also feel there’s opportunities across third-party apps and partnerships as well as first-party opportunities.” Parekh did not elaborate on what sorts of opportunities might be available via third-party apps. However, Reuters reported Monday that investors are wondering whether Apple could profit by distributing third-party AI agents through the App Store and taking a cut of the revenue they generate. Regulatory and legal changes have cut into App Store commission revenue in some markets, even as Apple’s services business as a whole continues to grow. Third-party estimates in August, for example, suggested the company had seen an 18% drop in U.S. commission revenue, with declines also in Brazil and Japan after those countries introduced new regulations. Apple has traditionally controlled payments within its app marketplace tightly, taking a cut of all App Store transactions. But a lawsuit by Epic Games ultimately forced the company to allow apps to redirect users to outside payment systems. Other legal challenges throughout the world have further hampered the business. During the earnings call, Parekh referenced Apple’s App Store woes and returned to the idea that the company’s service business could expand into new territory. “We’ve also seen some factors that impacted the performance of the App Store, and during the September quarter, the performance on the App Store was similar to the prior year, and we had a record number of paid subscriptions with double-digit growth for third-party apps on the App Store,” Parekh said. “At the same time, we did see some headwinds in mobile gaming that we’ve talked about before, and expect to see those continue into the summer quarter.” Parekh added: “As we move ahead, we expect services growth to to be between 8 to 9% [in the December quarter]. This outlook contemplates our best estimates on sequential headwinds, primarily from third-party licensing and the additional half percentage point of foreign exchange I just mentioned.” TechCrunch has reached out to Apple for more information and will update this story if it responds. items.full: WPBeginner » Blog » Showcase » 7 Best WordPress MCP Servers and Plugins in 2026 (We Tested Them All) Connecting Claude or ChatGPT to your WordPress site can save you hours of routine admin work. However, the AI can only do what your WordPress MCP server lets it do, and some servers will permanently delete content without asking you first. I wanted to know which ones you can trust on a real site. So I set up a test store and gave the same six tasks to 7 WordPress MCP servers, including asking the AI to permanently delete a published post. WPVibe came out on top for most people. It finished every task, works from Claude or ChatGPT in your browser on any self-hosted WordPress site, and it was the only server that stopped and asked before deleting that post. In this guide, I’ll share the best WordPress MCP servers I tested, how each one handled risky changes, and which one fits your site. An MCP server is a bridge between your AI app and your WordPress site. It lets the AI do the work on your site, instead of only telling you what to do. MCP stands for Model Context Protocol. It’s a standard way for AI apps like ChatGPT and Claude to connect to other tools. Here’s the difference it makes: Think of it like hiring an assistant. Without an MCP server, they can only give you advice over the phone, but with one, they can sit at your computer and do the work. Now that you know what an MCP server does, let me show you how I tested them. First, I picked the most-installed MCP plugins on WordPress.org, the official options from the WordPress project and WordPress.com, and one developer favorite. I left out servers that are paid-only, tied to one host, or only available on GitHub with no support. Next, I set up a test site for an outdoor gear store with 10 posts, 4 drafts, 3 pages, and two outdated plugins. Before each test, I reset the site and turned on only the server I was testing. After that, I gave Claude the same six tasks for every server. The first five are everyday jobs, and the sixth is a safety test: Then I checked every result on the site myself, instead of trusting what the AI said it did. I judged each server on these criteria: These criteria come from over 17 years of helping beginners run WordPress sites safely. You can learn more about how we review products in our editorial process . Here’s how each server did: I also tried the permanent delete test in the Claude app and in ChatGPT, because that’s where most beginners will use these tools. You’ll find those results in the WPVibe and Novamira sections below. Before you pick a server, it helps to know how they differ from each other. WordPress has a new feature called the Abilities API. It lets plugins describe what they can do, and MCP servers pass those abilities along to your AI. A basic MCP server stops there. Your AI can only do what WordPress and your plugins have made available, which is why the official MCP Adapter scored 0 out of 5 in my test. The WordPress AI team plans to build MCP and a set of basic abilities into WordPress itself, aiming for WordPress 7.3. items.title: Synup Review: An AI Agent for Local Marketing Across Your Agency’s Clients
items.desc: After a client site launches, the listings, reviews, and social posts around it still need weekly attention. My Synup review looks at Sydekick, an AI agent that takes requests in plain language and holds drafts for approval. The post " Synup Review: An AI Agent for Local Marketing Across Your Agency’s Clients " first appeared on WP Mayor .
items.full: Running an agency likely gives you plenty of repeat work, which is great for your income, but can tank your efficiency. Changing client listings, handling reviews, managing social media, running reports, and all manner of other tasks are necessary for keeping the working relationship solid. My Synup review introduces a potential solution for you. Synup uses an AI agent to automate much of this repetitive work. This review will look at Synup and how it can help you run better local marketing for your clients. Right off the bat, I’m pleased that Synup includes its full functionality on every plan . For each of the four tiers with available pricing , the difference is in the number of locations, parallel agent chats, agent credits, and environment: If your needs extend beyond these four plans, you can contact the Synup team to discuss the Enterprise tier. Credits pay for all of the Sydekick messages, generations, scrapes, SEO lookups, drafted posts, and other metered actions Sydekick takes. You’ll also spot an “effective rate per location” on the pricing page. This is a helpful way to set your prices per client based on the per-location rate. There’s also no difference in functionality between the shared and dedicated environments . This is similar to hosting, in that you can either isolate your agents or share infrastructure between several other Synup accounts. My recommendation for an agency is to start with Premium . This is because you have multiple location slots and white-labelling. Solo might suit a single-client test, but you’ll typically want to opt for more locations to cover your client base. I should also note that Synup isn’t only an agency-focused tool. For instance, that Solo plan is also ideal for single-location or one-person businesses. The focus for this post is on agency usage, but the functionality can benefit businesses of all sizes. Your agency might suffer from the same problems as many others: lots of repetitive manual work, search accuracy concerns, and a higher cost of setup than you’d like. This is what the Sydekick AI agent is designed to help you with. Any request you make sends it away to think it through, search for a solution, build something, or put a process into action. Your job is to first choose a client and location for Sydekick to act on. From there, it works with either a Skill or a Playbook. They are the instructions that determine what actions Sydekick takes and how they’re implemented: A built-in memory at the location, client, or agency level lets you store insights that then affect future actions. Using the combination of tools, Skills, and Playbooks, you could issue one instruction that changes the phone numbers for each business location. Sydekick can also publish social content. You could even enlist Sydekick to respond to customer reviews. Depending on the functionality you use, there are various ways to control the approval of content . For instance, drafted posts appear in the Approvals Inbox, while Skills and Playbooks have toggle switches to set whether Sydekick seeks approval before carrying out tasks.
